parole.testo: Unknown. The word is known to be recent, as the original word for morning in Finnish is huomen. It is likely that once huomen began to be used in words meaning "tomorrow", such as huominen and huomenna, it was eventually replaced by aamu in the sense "morning". One theory is that aamu is a shortenin
Borrowed from Old Swedish asne or asni (Swedish åsna), from Old French asne, from Latin asinus. Attested since the time of Mikael Agricola (output c. 1543–1552).

parole.significato: eve (day or night before, usually used for holidays)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish apton, afton (“evening, eve”); “evening” and “eve” are the same word in Swedish because the ecclesiastical day changes at 6 p.m., but only the sense “eve” has been borrowed into Finnish.
From Old Swedish almanacha, ultimately from Arabic الْمُنَاخ (al-munāḵ) through Medieval Latin almanachus.
Borrowed from Old Swedish altari, ultimately from Latin altare.

parole.significato: anchor (tool to hook a vessel into the seabed)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish [Term?] (whence Swedish ancker, a variant of ankare; compare Old Swedish ankæri, ankar; perhaps adapted with -uri), ultimately from Old Norse akkeri, from Proto-Germanic *ankurô, itself ultimately from Latin ancora.
From Old Swedish artogh (compare Swedish örtug).

parole.significato: a high official in Nordic countries whose main responsibility was to monitor the judiciary
parole.testo: From Old Swedish drotseti. Compare German Truchsess.
Borrowed from Old Swedish ängil, engil, from Latin angelus, from Ancient Greek ἄγγελος (ángelos).
Borrowed from Old Swedish ätika, ultimately from Latin acētum.
Borrowed from Old Swedish harnisk, compare modern Swedish harnesk, English harness.

parole.significato: hand net, sweep net (small net equipped with a handle and attached to a rim)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish hāver (whence Swedish håv), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hēbaz. Doublet of havas.

parole.significato: paddock, corral, croft (enclosure for livestock to graze in, especially one with deciduous trees)
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Old Swedish hagha, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hagô (“enclosure, yard; pasture”).

parole.significato: palisade (wall of wooden stakes, used as a defensive barrier)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hakul- (in Old Swedish hakulverk).

parole.significato: shot (small metal ball used as ammunition)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish haghl, from Proto-Germanic *haglaz.

parole.significato: A strong feeling of pleasure, especially of sexual kind.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish hägome (compare Icelandic hégómi).
From Old Swedish hælgho daghar (literally “holy days”).
From Old Swedish hælffwætte and Swedish helvete (“hell”).
Borrowed from Old Swedish hosa.

parole.significato: to rest, to have a break
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hvila, compare Modern Swedish vila.
Borrowed from Old Swedish hunagh, from Proto-Germanic *hunagą. Displaced mesi.
Borrowed from Old Swedish ia, iā (“yes”) (compare Swedish ja).
Borrowed from Old Swedish iarl, from Old Norse jarl, from Proto-Norse ᛖᚱᛁᛚᚨᛉ (erilaʀ), from Proto-Germanic *erlaz.

parole.significato: A member of a race of giants.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish *iatul (compare Old Swedish iætun, Norwegian jøtul), from Old Norse jǫtunn.
Potentially from an Old Swedish word corresponding to modern Swedish gäck (“clown”), extracted from sayings such as spela gäck (“to play a joke on someone”).

parole.significato: cabinet, closet, cupboard (a piece of furniture used for storage and closed with a door)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish skāp (compare modern Swedish skåp), from Middle Low German schap.
Borrowed from Old Swedish kāpa (compare modern Swedish kåpa and Icelandic kápa).
Borrowed from Old Swedish kalker, from Old French calice, from Latin calix, from Ancient Greek κᾰ́λῠξ (kắlŭx). First attested in 1469 (as Calci).
Borrowed from Old Swedish kamar (compare Swedish kammare (“room, chamber”)).

parole.significato: synonym of kokka (“bow of a boat”)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish kana.
From Old Swedish karsker.

parole.significato: street (paved part of road in a village or a town, especially one bordered by pavements or sidewalks)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish gata, from Old Norse gata, from Proto-Germanic *gatwǭ.
Possibly from keikka + -ari or from Old Swedish *gīgare.
Borrowed from Old Swedish keysar, keysare, from Middle Low German keiser, from Old High German keisar, keisur, from Proto-Germanic *kaisaraz, from Latin Caesar. Doublet of tsaari.

parole.significato: pike pole used in timber rafting or log driving
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish käxe (“hook”) (compare Swedish käx).
Borrowed from Old Swedish gæster (compare Swedish gäst (“guest”)). First attested in 1469 (as gesti).
Borrowed from Old Swedish gilde.

parole.significato: examination in rural areas held historically to teach and test literacy and knowledge of Christianity, now used chiefly…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish gingerdh, gengiärdh.
Borrowed from Old Swedish skipari.
Borrowed from Old Swedish kirvil, itself borrowed from Middle Low German kervele, ultimately from Latin caerefolium, from Ancient Greek χαιρέφυλλον (khairéphullon).

parole.significato: any plant of the genus Solanum, including nightshades, tomato, potato, eggplant etc.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kvesa. Originally in the sense "ulcer, cancer"; in the modern plant sense through koisonheinä (+ heinä).
Possibly borrowed from Old Swedish qwiþa.
Borrowed from Old Swedish kokker (compare Swedish kock), from Old Saxon kok. First attested in 1458 (as Kocki).
Borrowed from Old Swedish korgh, korgher.
Borrowed from Old Swedish korper (compare Swedish korp), from Old Norse korpr. Displaced kaarne.
Borrowed from Old Swedish krogher (Swedish krog), from Middle Low German krōch.
Borrowed from Old Swedish hviska (“to whisper”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hwīskrōną.

parole.significato: chancel, apse (space around the altar in a church)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish kor, through Old Norse kórr from Latin chorus. Doublet of kuoro.
Borrowed from Old Swedish koppar. Has largely displaced native vaski.
Possibly from Old Swedish kuppa (“blister”).

Borrowed from Old Swedish kyndil (“candle, torch”) or older Old East Norse kyndill. Cognate to Estonian küünal, Ingrian kyntteli, Votic čüntteli. Ultimately from Latin candela, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kand- (“to shine, glow”). Doublet of kandela.

parole.significato: someone who keeps watching, sniffs around, is meddlesome; a busybody
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish skytta (“shooter”) (compare Swedish skytte).

parole.significato: ride, lift (act of transporting someone in a vehicle)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish skiut (compare Swedish skjuts), from Old Norse skjótr.
Borrowed from Old Swedish kärra, probably from Old Frisian [Term?], ultimately from Latin carrus, from Gaulish *karros, from Proto-Celtic *karros (“wagon”).

parole.significato: chief justice (unofficial English translation of the title of a judge serving as office chief of a District Court; also…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish laghman (compare modern Swedish lagman).

parole.significato: storage bin (especially for grain or other agricultural produce)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish lar (compare modern Swedish lår), from Old Norse lár. Akin to Russian ларь (larʹ) (also borrowed from Old Swedish or Old Norse).

parole.significato: adhesive bandage, band-aid (US); sticking plaster, plaster (UK)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish plaster (whence modern Swedish plåster), ultimately from Latin emplastrum.

Borrowed from Old Swedish ladhika (“small box”) (compare modern Swedish läddika and Danish læddike, lædike (“chest, box, drawer”)), from Middle Low German ladic, ladicke, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hlaþō (“drawer”) (compare German Lade, whence Hungarian láda, ládikó). The ending of the word is

parole.significato: slab (flat, broad piece of a relatively stiff material)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish plata (compare modern Swedish plåt).
Borrowed from Old Swedish slakta, from Middle Low German slachten.

Borrowed from Old Swedish slagh (whence Swedish slag (“kind, sort”)), from Middle Low German slach, from Proto-West Germanic *slagi, from Proto-Germanic *slagiz (whence also Swedish slag (“hit, punch, blow”), as inherited from Old Norse). Doublet of laes.

parole.significato: act (a specific legal statute, inferior to a constitution)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish lagh (compare Swedish lag), from Old Norse lǫg.

parole.significato: flagon, flask (Uusimaa, Kymenlaakso, Central Finland, Savonia, North Karelia, South Karelia)
parole.testo: < Old Swedish flaska

parole.significato: play (activity for amusement only, especially among the young)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish leker (compare Swedish lek, Old Norse leikr).

parole.significato: flagon (vessel of about 2 to 3 liters, used for drink, in Finland made primarily of wood, elsewhere also of leather, me…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish läghil, from Latin lagēna, from Ancient Greek λᾰ́γῡνος (lắgūnos). Compare Swedish lägel.

Borrowed from Old Swedish lilia, from Old Norse lilja, from Medieval Latin līlia, plural of līlium, from Ancient Greek λείριον (leírion), from Fayyumic Coptic ϩⲗⲏⲣⲓ (hlēri) (compare Sahidic Coptic ϩⲣⲏⲣⲉ (hrēre)), from Demotic Egyptian (ḥrry), from Egyptian Hr:r-r:*t-M2 (ḥrrt, “flower”). Compare mode

parole.significato: line (a connected set of points, e.g. a path acting as a boundary)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish linia (compare modern Swedish linje), from Latin līnea.

lohi- + käärme (“snake, serpent”). Originally a variant of louhikäärme (“louhi-serpent”), a partial calque of Old Swedish floghdraki; see louhikäärme for more. The initial component has become associated with lohi (“salmon”) by folk etymology.

parole.significato: the upper floor of a granary or similar structure
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish lufft, from Old Norse lopt.

parole.significato: A church officer, similar to a sexton.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish klukkare or klokkare (compare modern Swedish klockare).

parole.significato: abbey, cloister; (for monks) monastery; (for nuns) convent, nunnery
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kloster, ultimately from Latin claustrum.
Borrowed from Old Swedish lodh or directly from Middle Low German lōt, from Proto-West Germanic *laud.
Borrowed from Old Swedish plōma (whence modern Swedish plommon). Ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *plūmā.
Borrowed from Old Swedish blȳ, from Old Norse blý, from Proto-Germanic *blīwiją.
Borrowed from Old Swedish lyst, itself from Middle Low German lüst, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *lustuz.
From Old Swedish läkia + -itä (compare modern Swedish läka (“to heal”)), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *lēkinōną.
Borrowed from Old Swedish lø̄s, from Old Norse lauss, from Proto-Germanic *lausaz. A doublet of lössi, lausas, lauha.

parole.significato: painter (one who paints, e.g. walls or other surfaces)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish mālare. Analyzable as maalata (“to paint”) + -ari (“-er”).
Borrowed from Old Swedish māla (“to paint”) (compare Swedish måla and German malen). Analyzable as maali (“paint”) + -ata. Compare Karelian mualata.
Borrowed from Old Swedish māl (“paint”), from māla (“to paint”), itself borrowed from Middle Low German mâlen (“to paint”), from Proto-Germanic *mēlijaną (“to mark, stain, paint”).

Borrowed from Old Swedish māl (“measure, amount; sign”) (compare Swedish mål (“target; what one aims to hit”)), from both Old Norse mál (“language, speech”) (from Proto-Germanic *maþlą) and Old Norse mál (“size, measurement, time”) (from Proto-Germanic *mēlą).
maan (“country's, land's”, genitive) + tie (“road”), probably a calque of Old Swedish landsvægher (whence Swedish landsväg).
Borrowed from Old Swedish marknaþer (compare Swedish marknad).
Borrowed from Old Swedish mast, from Proto-Germanic *mastaz (whence also English mast).
< Old Swedish mær
Borrowed from Old Swedish mærki (compare modern Swedish märke), from Old Norse merki, from Proto-Germanic *markō.
Borrowed from Old Swedish [Term?] (compare modern Swedish mässa).

parole.significato: master (person with extensive skill or ability; one who has mastered something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish mæstare (compare Swedish mästare). First attested in 1380 (in Muremestare). Doublet of maisteri.
Borrowed from Old Swedish mesta, mista (“to lose possession of”); the main sense further influenced by similar-sounding mästerman (“executioner”).
From Old Swedish miþsumar (“midsummer”).
Borrowed from Old Swedish manadha koster (“food provision for one month”) (compare Swedish månadskost) and clipped. First attested in 1422 (in Monapyrthe).

parole.significato: mould/mold (hollow form or matrix for shaping a fluid or plastic substance)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish mōt (“mold, cast”), from Old Norse mót. Doublet of muoto.

parole.significato: wall (rampart built for defensive purposes; structure built for defense)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish mur (compare Swedish mur, German Mauer), ultimately from Latin murus. First attested in 1380 (in Muremestare).
Borrowed from Old Swedish mylla, mylna (compare Icelandic mylla and German Mühle), ultimately from Latin molina.

parole.significato: miller (an operator or owner of a mill)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish myllare, mylnare, ultimately from Latin molinarius. By surface analysis, mylly + -äri.
Borrowed from Old Swedish mänta (“alum leather”) (compare Swedish mänta). First attested in 1405 (in Mentinpoyca). The sense referring to a person may be re-extracted from the compound mänttipää.
Borrowed from Old Swedish nappa (“to bite, to take”), from Proto-Germanic *hnappōną.
Borrowed from Old Swedish knapper (compare Swedish knapp). First attested in 1459 (in Napin kifvi).
Borrowed from Old Swedish snidhkare (compare Swedish snickare (“carpenter”)). First attested in 1411 (in Nikkarinpoyka).

parole.significato: a peasant appointed as the representative of a rural municipality (pitäjä)
parole.testo: By syncope from earlier nimitysmies (compare obsolete nimitzmies), from nimitys (“appointment”) + mies (“man”), a kind of calque of Old Swedish nempdaman (literally “appointed man”).

parole.significato: stake, pole, stanchion, picket, pale (long and slender piece of wood or other material, often pointed at one end so as…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish pāl, pāle (compare modern Swedish påle; cognate with English pole); ultimately from Latin pālus.

parole.significato: stretcher (simple litter designed to carry a sick, injured, or dead person)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish bār (compare modern Swedish bår (“stretcher”)).

parole.significato: fast (act or practice of abstaining from or eating very little food)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish fasta, fasto (“fast”).
Borrowed from Old Swedish bāter (“boat”) (compare modern Swedish båt).
Borrowed from Old Swedish pavi, pave (“pope”) (compare modern Swedish påve), from Old Norse páfi, from Old Saxon pābos, pāvos, from Old French pape, from Ecclesiastical Latin pāpa.
Uncertain; possibly borrowed from Old Swedish baker. Related to Ingrian pakkaara and Kukkuzi pakara.
Borrowed from Old Swedish balder, baller. For the sense "ball, testicle", compare Old Norse bǫllr (“a ball”), whence Icelandic böllur (“scrotum; penis; a ball”). Doublet of pallo.
Borrowed from Old Swedish banna, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bannaną.

parole.significato: a couple of (about two, certainly more than one but not much more than three)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish par, from Middle Low German par, from Latin pār (whence also English pair, Spanish par). * (par (in finance)): Likely a semantic loan from Italian pari.
Borrowed from Old Swedish pil, pijl, ultimately from Latin pīlum.
Borrowed from Old Swedish pina, itself borrowed through Middle Low German pīn, pīne, from Latin poena, from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ). Compare Danish pine, Estonian piin.
Borrowed from Old Swedish bisp, a shortened form of biskop, ultimately from Latin episcopus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos).
Borrowed from Old Swedish bikar(e) (compare modern Swedish bägare).

Borrowed from Old Swedish bik, from Middle Low German pik, from Latin pix. The e-stem, unusual for a borrowing as recent as this, is probably by analogy with hiki in order to avoid problematic homonymous forms such as *piin (~ piin, genitive of pii).
Borrowed from Old Swedish spil, from Middle Low German spil, from Proto-West Germanic *spil. Cognates include Estonian pila, Karelian pila. Doublet of peli.
pipar- + juuri; partial calque of Old Swedish piparrot (the initial element of which is also the source of pippuri).

Borrowed from Old Swedish piper, pipper (perhaps adapted with -uri), from Old Norse piparr, from Latin piper (“pepper”), from Ancient Greek πέπερι (péperi, “pepper”), from an Indo-Aryan source; compare Sanskrit पिप्पलि (pippali, “long pepper”).
From Old Swedish biur.
From Old Swedish boghi.
Borrowed from Old Swedish borghare. Sense 2 is a semantic loan from French bourgeois.
Borrowed from Old Swedish pundari (compare modern Swedish pyndare).

parole.significato: bag (small, flexible container for items; made of e.g. paper or plastic, either for packaging or storage, or for carryi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish pusi, posi (compare modern Swedish påse), from Proto-Germanic *pusô.
Borrowed from Old Swedish byssa (compare modern Swedish bössa (“gun, rifle”), Icelandic byssa (“gun”)).

parole.significato: A post that is used to mark something, especially a border or limit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish [Term?] (compare dialectal Swedish pyk (“small pile or heap”)). First attested in 1424 (in Kifwipijckihin).
Borrowed from Old Swedish bōk (compare Swedish bok).

parole.significato: A settled place, a settlement (found mainly in place names).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish bøle.
From Old Swedish böfvel (“executioner”), compare modern Swedish bödel.
Borrowed from Old Swedish dragha; compare modern Swedish draga. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *draganą.
Probably borrowed from Old Swedish rakke (“dog”), compare Swedish racka.
Borrowed from Old Swedish skræppa (whence modern Swedish skräppa (“leather sack, leather bag”)).
Borrowed from Old Swedish grīma (among its meanings, "halter; (dialectal) mark in wood"; compare Swedish grimma (“halter”)), from Proto-Germanic *grīmô. Cognate with Estonian kriim.
Borrowed from Old Swedish drīva.

parole.significato: confession (disclosure of one's sins to a priest)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish skript, from Latin scriptus. Doublet of skripti.
Either a back-formation from risahtaa, like etymology 2, and/or a borrowing from Old Swedish bris, vris (whence Swedish bräss and also related to German Bries).
From Old Swedish trumpare. The -l- is by later dissimilation.
Borrowed from Old Swedish rūm (“room, space”).
From Old Swedish rädikia. Doublet of retikka.
From Old Swedish sakerstige; adapted with -sto.

Probably borrowed from Old Swedish sangare (“singer”). Compare with Väinämöinen, the singing hero. Another theory suggests it is derived from the verb sangata or sankailla, ("to resist, to defy, threaten"). Can be related to the words sankka, sakea, sangen (compare voimakas).
Borrowed from Old Swedish säppel, säppal, ultimately from Early Medieval Latin cappellus. Doublet of säppäli.

parole.significato: soul (spirit or essence of a person or of a thing)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish siel, siäl (“soul”) (compare modern Swedish själ, German Seele, English soul), from Old Saxon sēola, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *saiwalō.

parole.significato: harness saddle (part of a horse harness; a band passing over the horse's back, often with pads, that support the weight…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish sili.

parole.significato: silk (fine fiber excreted by the silkworm)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish silke, Old Norse silki, ultimately from Latin sēricus (see it and English silk for further etymology).
Borrowed from Old Swedish sighna (compare Swedish signa), ultimately from Latin signō.
From Old Swedish spital.
Borrowed from Old Swedish sōt (“soot”).
From Old Swedish swagher (modern Swedish svåger).
Borrowed from Old Swedish sutare (“cobbler, shoemaker”), from Latin sūtor (“cobbler, shoemaker”).
Borrowed from Old Swedish sylta (compare Swedish sylta). First attested in 1414 (as Sylthy).
Borrowed from Old Swedish synd (compare Swedish synd).

parole.significato: A pension-like arrangement in which a former owner of a property retains the right to dwell in some part of the propert…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish syting.

parole.significato: sack (large bag for storage and handling)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish sækker (compare Swedish säck), from Proto-Germanic *sakkuz (“sack”), from Latin saccus (“large bag”), from Ancient Greek σάκκος (sákkos, “bag of coarse cloth”), from Semitic. First attested in 1323 (in the place name Sekiierue, modern Säkkijärvi).

parole.significato: bread roll, roll, bun (type of bread)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish sembla, sämbla (compare Swedish semla), from Middle Low German sēmele, semmel, semmele, from Proto-West Germanic *similā, from Latin simila (“the finest flour”).

parole.significato: a decorated broadcloth circlet/schapel, traditional Karelian female headwear
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish säppal. Doublet of seppele.
From Old Swedish säter, from Middle Low German sēter. Originally referred to any fine fabric in general. The sense "rayon silk" is a neologism from the 1930s.
From taka- + -ta. Probably also influenced by or alternatively even borrowed from Old Swedish taka or earlier.

parole.significato: coat, jacket (piece of clothing worn on the upper body outside a shirt or blouse, covering the upper torso and arms)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish stakker, compare Icelandic stakkur (“coat”), from Proto-Germanic *stakkaz (“short jacket”).

parole.significato: to beat with a carpetbeater (to remove dust)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish damba (compare Swedish damma, damm (“dust”)).

parole.significato: pocket (bag stitched to an item of clothing)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish taska, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *taskǭ (probably through Middle Low German).

Borrowed from Old Swedish diäkn, deghn, compare Swedish djäkne, ultimately from Ancient Greek διάκονος (diákonos). The historical senses listed below are the original one. The sense “teen” is taken from English teen and the Finnish word is sometimes considered to originate from the English one, even
Borrowed from Old Swedish þiǣna, þiēna, compare modern Swedish tjäna (“to earn”).

Borrowed from Old Swedish þiǣnist, thienst, þiānist (“service, decoration of honor”), from Proto-Germanic *þewanōstaz (“service”). Akin to Swedish tjänst (“service; employment, job, esp. public office”), German Dienst, Dutch dienst.
Borrowed from Old Swedish tighl, from Old Norse tigl, from Proto-Germanic *tigulǭ, from Latin tēgula.
Borrowed from Old Swedish tīme.

parole.significato: Tuesday (day of the week; the second day of the week in Finland and in the ISO 8601 standard)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish tisdagher (or another North Germanic language), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *Tīwas dag.
tika- + -ri, perhaps a blend of two now obsolete words tikaveitsi and takari; ultimately thus perhaps a blend of Old Swedish stikämäz and Old Swedish [Term?] (compare dialectal Swedish daggare).
tika- + -as (initial component also found in tikapuut), borrowed from Old Swedish stighi (compare dialectal Swedish stiga).

parole.significato: Old Finnish unit of amount; ten squirrel furs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish dikur, from Middle Low German deker, from Latin decuria.

parole.significato: account (in a bank, a registry of pecuniary transactions; on a service, an authorization to use a service)
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Old Swedish (planko) thili (“wooden boards”). Accounts were once recorded on tally sticks, which resemble wooden boards. Alternatively related to tila.
Borrowed from Old Swedish þing, from Old East Norse [Term?], from Old Norse þing, from Proto-Germanic *þingą.

Borrowed from Old Swedish torgh, from Old Norse torg, itself borrowed from Old East Slavic търгъ (tŭrgŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tъrgъ. Compare Faroese torg, Icelandic torg, Norwegian Bokmål torg, Norwegian Nynorsk torg, Swedish torg. Doublet of turku.

parole.significato: log, stock (heavy, usually round piece of lumber)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish stokker (“tree trunk, log”) (compare modern Swedish stock).

parole.significato: interpreter (person who translates speech or signing from one language to another)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish tolker, itself ultimately borrowed from Proto-Slavic *tъlkъ, probably from Proto-Indo-European *telkʷ-. * (gauge): Also found in Swedish tolk, possibly a later semantic loan.
Borrowed from Old Swedish stund (compare Swedish stund, German Stunde).
Borrowed from Old Swedish stōl. The older form stuoli can still be found in some compounds (such as saarnastuoli).

parole.significato: barrel, keg, vat, cask, drum (cylindrical hollow container for liquids)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish tynnor, the plural of tynna; compare Swedish tunna (“barrel”). See English tun for further etymology.
Borrowed from Old Swedish thäkän (“rug, blanket”).

parole.significato: oven (chamber used for baking or heating)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish ughn (“oven”) (compare modern Swedish ugn).

parole.significato: scales, scale (device to measure mass or weight)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish vāgh (compare Swedish våg (“scale”)), from Old Norse vág, from Proto-Germanic *wēgō. See also väkä.

parole.significato: coat of arms, insignia, arms, escutcheon (of a family, state, etc.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish vaakn, vakn, variants of Old Swedish vapn (“coat of arms”) (compare modern Swedish vapen).
Borrowed from Old Swedish fange (compare Swedish fånge), itself from Middle Low German vangen (“captive”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *fangōną.
Borrowed from Old Swedish vaghn (compare modern Swedish vagn), from Old Norse vagn, from Proto-Germanic *wagnaz.

parole.significato: bet, wager (an instance of making a bet)
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Old Swedish væþ, vedh, from Old Norse veð, from Proto-Germanic *wadją. Also associated with veto (etymology 1).

parole.significato: to marry, wed, join in holy matrimony (to perform the ceremony of joining spouses)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish vighia (compare modern Swedish viga).
Borrowed from Old Swedish viller.

parole.significato: post, position, office, public office (public sector work, e.g. civil service work)
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Old Swedish virke, with possible influence from virka (etymology 2) with which it has been equated in the past.
Borrowed from Old Swedish viþia. Doublet of vitsa.
Borrowed from Old Swedish fougde (“bailiff”).

parole.significato: lining (covering for the inside of a garment)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish fōþer, compare modern Swedish foder.
Probably borrowed from Old Swedish væghia (compare Swedish väja (“to give way, make way, swerve”)), perhaps implying an earlier form *väɣjä- (compare dialectal väijätä).

Borrowed from Old Swedish yrt (modern Swedish ört), from Old Norse urt, oblique case form of Proto-Germanic *wrōts, from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds (“root”). Compare English wort, root and Latin rādīx (“root”).
Borrowed from Old Swedish olia, olea (compare Swedish olja, dialectal (Finland) Swedish öljo, and German Öl), ultimately from Latin oleum, from Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, “olive oil”).
